title: Pim's Perilous Parcel
markdown:
The mountain air tasted of pine needles, crisp and clean with a hint of something wild. Goblin Pim, emerald-green nose twitching, clutched a lumpy parcel wrapped in glistening damp moss. Elder Grumbles had pressed it into his small hands with a serious nod. “To the Mountain King, Pim. Before the moon is a perfect circle. It’s vital.” Elder Grumbles’ words were as reliable as sunrise. Deliver the package to the reclusive King high in the granite peaks before moonrise. Pim, master of every secret path on the Cliffside Paths, thought it should be easy.

Goblin’s Perch was a jumble of cleverness and stubborn rock: tiny houses like colourful toadstools clinging to sheer faces, rope bridges of vine and spider silk, contraptions whirring on mountain wind and gurgling streams. Deep green pines, cliffside lanterns winking like sleepy stars — Pim’s grandest playground. Today a new melody joined the usual sounds, so pure the pinecones hummed.

Around a sharp bend, bathed in a sunbeam, sat an elf with a lute: tall, slender, hair like spun moonlight, eyes the colour of forest pools. He introduced himself as Aerion, voice a soft breeze through leaves. “A parcel, you say? And where must it journey, little goblin?”

Before Pim could answer, a colossal shadow blotted the sun. A dragon, scales emerald, wings like stained glass, landed with a soft thud. Pearly smoke smelled faintly of toasted marshmallows. “Greetings, small folk,” boomed Ignis, thunder with warmth. “What requires my esteemed assistance?”

Pim clutched the parcel. “Just delivering this. To the King. Before the moon is full.”

Ignis rumbled. “A chasm, perhaps? Allow me.” He nudged an enormous jagged boulder toward the path’s edge. “A bridge of sorts. Perfectly adequate for someone of your stature.”

Pim’s jaw dropped. The boulder would obliterate the narrow trail. This was not help. “No, thank you, Mr Dragon, sir. I have my own ways. And besides,” a cheeky grin, pointing to a nearly invisible path snaking down the cliff, “Elder Grumbles specifically said no boulder bridges.”

Aerion watched with a knowing smile. Ignis blinked golden eyes. “Ah. My enthusiasm sometimes outpaces my practicality. Perhaps a flight? I could deposit you upon the King’s doorstep with a mere beat of wings.”

“Too risky for the parcel. It’s fragile.” Pim was already scampering down the hidden path.

Aerion followed. “A tricky path indeed.”

“That’s the fun part.” On a narrow ledge a tiny long-eared creature darted from a crevice, scampered up Pim’s tunic, and latched on. Pim scooped it gently. “You’ve got spirit. You can come too.” He named the rock-hopper Pip. It snuggled into his neck.

Ignis, full of ideas, tried weaving a bridge of clouds and hopeful wishes, then bellowed about updrafts and sent a playful hurricane. Pim and Aerion dodged. Pip clung. Aerion’s lute sang a frantic song of gusts and surprised elf-notes.

The chasm loomed, vast and deep. The usual rickety rope bridge looked particularly perilous. Ignis reappeared. “The traditional method. Allow me to stabilize it.” He produced a giant shimmering feather. “Placed strategically, it will eliminate all sway.” He dropped it. It sailed past the bridge and disappeared with a faint plink into the abyss.

The sun dipped. Moss turned a deep bruised purple. Pip chittered. Aerion’s calm became thoughtful concern.

Then a strong gust from Ignis’s well-meaning chaos snatched the parcel from Pim’s grasp. Almost at the same time Ignis, trying to catch it with a massive paw, overbalanced and swept Aerion toward the chasm’s edge.

“No.” Parcel, mission, Aerion — slipping. A cold dread settled in Pim’s small chest.

Aerion dangled, lute clutched. The parcel spun. Pip, on Pim’s shoulder, chirped a brave defiant sound. Pim remembered the village contraptions, problems solved with wit and scraps. He was not just a messenger. He was a goblin inventor. Aerion, even in peril, was watching, assessing.

“Aerion. The pine trees. The sticky sap.”

Aerion’s eyes widened. While Ignis flustered below, trying to grow a ladder of moonbeams that vanished, Aerion used his lute to redirect a gentle gust, nudging Pim toward pines clinging to the cliff. With Pip’s uncanny grip and his own nimble fingers, Pim slid down a rope, gathering sticky amber sap.

“Pip, grab on.” Pip gripped the sap-covered parcel like a tiny anchor. Pim swung from a thick pine branch and launched parcel and Pip across the gap. A triumphant squeak. Safe landing.

“The King’s tower,” Aerion shouted, pointing to a warmly lit spire. “Ignis. A focused gust, just below the parcel. Not a hurricane. A gentle nudge.”

Ignis, humbled, obliged. A precise puff guided the parcel toward the entrance. Pim scrambled after it, Aerion following with a soaring melody. They reached the King’s grand antechamber as the moon, a perfect silver coin, reached its zenith. An ancient goblin, crown of polished river stones, accepted the parcel with a knowing smile.

“You have delivered,” the King rumbled. “Resourcefulness, not brute strength.”

Ignis bowed, emerald scales dimming. “My apologies for overzealous assistance. My intentions were good. My execution, perhaps too grand.”

Pim grinned, Pip perched proudly. Aerion strummed a gentle contented tune. The mountain lanterns flickered, the same sleepy-star wink as Goblin’s Perch, only now they marked a parcel delivered by a path no boulder could improve.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
